objective: Measure S3's rebalance timing luck across 21 signal-day offsets and test whether a four-tranche version lowers drawdown without giving up Sharpe or the G1 bar.

sources.core_claim: In a concentrated (20-stock) monthly-rebalanced US momentum portfolio, 1991-2024, the CAGR gap between the best and worst trading day of the month was 348 bp; splitting into 2-20 tranches left the mean CAGR (16.7-16.8%) and Sharpe (0.59-0.60) unchanged while shrinking the dispersion from 3.48% to 0-2%. Single-day max drawdowns ranged -69.3% to -74.9%.
sources.project_applicability: Closest published analogue to S3: concentrated, monthly, momentum. Sets the prior that tranching changes dispersion, not the mean.
sources.reflection: Full PDF read (tables 1 and 3). It reports no drawdown for tranched books, so the drawdown question is exactly the local gap.

sources.core_claim: Factor indices (value, size, momentum, quality, low vol) show rebalance timing luck often above 100 bp annualized, larger for concentrated and less frequently rebalanced portfolios.
sources.project_applicability: Confirms RTL is large for concentrated monthly books; S3 holds two ETFs, the most concentrated case.
sources.reflection: Abstract only; the PDF was blocked.

sources.core_claim: Equal-weighting N staggered sub-portfolios suppresses rebalance timing luck roughly by 1/N (Hoffstein, Sibears, Faber, Journal of Beta Investment Strategies 2019), per CXO Advisory's summary.
sources.project_applicability: Gives the mechanism for T4: four staggered tranches should cut the dispersion to about a quarter.

sources.core_claim: Tranched rebalancing behaves like strategic rebalancing plus a slow trend-following component, because each tranche reacts at a different date.
sources.project_applicability: Counter-hypothesis for S3: tranching slows the switch to SHY in a fast crash (only a quarter of the book moves at each date), which could deepen drawdowns.
sources.reflection: Conceptual payoff diagrams, no empirical table.

sources.core_claim: Defines rebalance timing luck as the dispersion between identical portfolios rebalanced on different dates and recommends equal-weight exposure to sub-indexes.

On a timing-luck-sensitive TAA strategy (Bold Asset Allocation), tranched portfolios averaged 14.2% a year against 13.9% for single-day ones, and the spread of possible annual returns fell by almost two thirds.
sources.project_applicability: Practitioner record that the tranched mean return matches single-day books.

sources.core_claim: Tranching a timing-luck-sensitive TAA strategy makes performance more predictable.
sources.project_applicability: Earlier practitioner evidence; the site now lets members tranche live models.

sources.core_claim: Twenty offset versions of a long-only S&P 500 momentum strategy spread widely; the averaged sub-portfolio result lies between the best and worst.
sources.project_applicability: Independent small replication on long-only momentum.

sources.core_claim: TAA investors trading only at month end carry timing luck; split the book and trade each part on a different day.
sources.project_applicability: Month-end is exactly S3's live convention.

candidate_matrix_revisions.effect: Offsets 0-20 sessions after month end (one full month of trading days) as a descriptive distribution, not a menu to pick from; the live O00 stays the reference and no offset can be adopted on its own.
Four tranches (0/5/10/15) rather than 20: enough to cut dispersion to about a quarter while keeping at most one small order set per week on a $15k sleeve.
Pass rule requires shallower max drawdown in BOTH anchor and stress, because the slower reaction of a tranched book could deepen a fast crash.
